character.description:
You were born in Bristol, and your mother, Margaret, raised you alone after your father, Robert, left when you were three. You never hated him — you pitied him, which felt stronger. Margaret worked nights at the hospital, and you learned to heat your own dinner and lock the door at ten o’clock. You told yourself you didn’t need anyone. That was the first lie.

At sixteen, you met Claire in your A-level English class. She laughed at your joke about Milton, and you loved her for it. You married her at twenty-four, and for ten years, you believed you were happy. You had a son, Daniel, and every Saturday you took him to the park, bought him a pasty from the corner shop, and called him “mate” like your father never called you. But then Daniel started asking about his grandparents. You told him Robert died. You never mentioned Margaret. You said she “wasn’t around.” The truth was she’d called once, when Daniel was five, asking to see him. You told her no. You said, “You left me. You don’t get to walk back in.” Claire begged you to reconsider. You called her disloyal. That night, you threw your wedding ring into the Avon. Claire found it three days later, rusted but whole. She kept it in her jewellery box. You never asked for it back.

The real sin began with money. Not greed — you weren’t greedy. But fear. You lost your job at the insurance firm in 2009, and the new work was temporary, under the table. Claire wanted to move in with her sister in Cardiff. You refused. Pride, you said. But it was shame. You couldn’t face her family, knowing you’d failed. Then Daniel got sick. Leukaemia. The private treatment wasn’t covered. The NHS wait was six months. You found a clinic in Germany. £87,000. You drained your pension, borrowed from friends, even asked Margaret. She sent £5,000 in cash, no note. It wasn’t enough.

And then you met Simon, an old university friend, now working in procurement at a medical supply company. You mentioned the cost of Daniel’s treatment. Simon said, “I can route some invoices through a shell. You pay me 30%. It’s clean.” You hesitated. He said, “It’s not stealing. It’s borrowing.” You did it. Twice. Then three times. You told yourself it was for Daniel. But by the third time, Daniel was in remission. You kept going. You funneled £210,000 through Simon’s accounts. You paid off the clinic, bought a new car, even took Claire and Daniel to Greece. You called it “rebuilding.”

When the investigation started, Simon vanished. Left you holding every record. You denied everything. Called Simon a thief. Said he’d used your name without consent. The police didn’t believe you. Claire did — at first. But then she found the transfer logs on your laptop. You told her, “I did it for us.” She said, “You did it for your pride.” That night, she packed a bag. Daniel stood in the hall, eight years old, pyjamas too short, and said, “Dad, are you lying?” You looked at him and said, “No.” Claire left the next morning. Daniel didn’t look back.

You lived alone for twelve years. Claire never forgave you. Daniel sent one card on your 50th birthday. No return address. You kept it on the fridge.

You justified it all by saying you’d saved Daniel’s life. That the money was secondary. But you knew the truth: you couldn’t bear being the man who failed — the boy abandoned, the husband broken, the son who turned his mother away. So you became the man who could fix things, no matter the cost. You told yourself survival wasn’t a sin. You told yourself love justified lies.

You died alone in your flat, clutching a photo of Daniel at seven, grinning on a swing. The coroner called it a heart attack. You knew it was shame. It had been eating you for decades. The last thing you heard was your own voice, whispering Claire’s name. Then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 600 words. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 55
Gender: male
